questionText: What is encapsulation, and how does it differ from abstraction?
shortAnswer: Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that operate on it and hides internals (private fields, public intent-revealing API). Abstraction exposes what an object does while hiding how. Encapsulation is the mechanism; abstraction is the resulting simplified view.
detailedAnswer: Encapsulation: a BankAccount exposes Deposit/Withdraw and hides balance validation, pending-transaction lists, and overdraft rules — misuse becomes unrepresentable (you cannot set a negative balance because no setter exists). Achieved via access modifiers (private/protected/internal), properties with asymmetric access (public get, private set), and keeping invariants inside the class (constructors establish them, methods preserve them). Abstraction: the caller sees IOrderService.Place(order) without knowing about inventory, payment, or email — what, not how. Interfaces and abstract classes are abstraction tools; private members are encapsulation tools. Tellisketch's rule: ask what the object guarantees, not what it stores. Code smells of broken encapsulation: anemic models with public setters everywhere + logic in services (procedural code in OO clothing), train-wreck chains (order.Customer.Address.Zip set from outside — the object should expose RelocateTo(address) instead), and primitive obsession leaking domain rules into callers.
internalWorking: No runtime machinery — encapsulation is a compile-time visibility contract (metadata flags the CLR enforces for direct access; reflection can bypass, which is why libraries must not rely on privacy for security). The payoff is entirely in maintainability: hidden members can change without recompiling callers (when kept behind stable properties/methods).
realWorldUsage: Domain entities guarding invariants, value objects (Money with currency checks), API request models with private setters + constructors, and framework classes that keep caches/locks private.
commonMistake: Public auto-properties for everything (anemic domain model), then duplicating validation in every service. Also: protected fields (subclasses couple to representation — prefer protected methods/properties).
technicalConversation: Ask what invariant their favorite entity guarantees and where it is enforced — if the answer is 'in the service layer', encapsulation has leaked.
interviewFollowUp: How do records with init-only properties change the encapsulation conversation?
keyTakeaway: Encapsulation hides how and protects invariants; abstraction simplifies what. Make illegal states unrepresentable.

questionText: How do virtual, override, abstract, and new differ in C# inheritance?
shortAnswer: virtual + override = runtime polymorphism (most-derived implementation wins); abstract = no implementation, must override; new = hides the base member (compile-time, non-polymorphic — usually a warning sign); sealed stops further overriding.
detailedAnswer: virtual marks a member as dispatchable: calls resolve to the runtime type's override, enabling template-method patterns (base defines skeleton, subclasses fill steps). override replaces it (must match signature; cannot narrow access). abstract members have no body and force derived classes to implement (abstract classes cannot be instantiated; they may also carry concrete shared code — the difference from interfaces pre-C# 8). new (method hiding) creates an unrelated member with the same name: which runs depends on the compile-time type of the variable — order.Process() on an Order variable vs Payment variable behave differently. This breaks substitutability and the compiler warns (CS0108) precisely because it is almost never intended; fix by making the base virtual + override, or rename. sealed on an override/class stops further derivation (runtime devirtualization + design intent: string is sealed). Constructors are never inherited/virtual; static members hide but never override. Polymorphism also flows through interfaces (implicitly virtual) — the primary extensibility mechanism in modern C# (prefer composition + interfaces over deep hierarchies).
internalWorking: Virtual calls go through the method table (vtable) slot: the object's type pointer selects the implementation at runtime (one indirection; JIT devirtualizes sealed/final cases). new members get separate slots — overload resolution happens purely at compile time against the variable's static type.
realWorldUsage: Template method in frameworks (ControllerBase lifecycle), test doubles (virtual members enable Moq proxies — hence virtual on Ef Core navigations), and plugin base classes with abstract hooks.
commonMistake: new to 'fix' a warning without understanding hiding (behavior changes with cast), forgetting to mark test-seam methods virtual (unmockable), and deep hierarchies where composition + strategy would isolate change better.
technicalConversation: Ask them to predict the output of the LegacyPayment snippet before running it — the surprise is the lesson, and it tests whether they respect compiler warnings.
interviewFollowUp: Why does Moq require virtual members, and what does that imply about sealed classes?
keyTakeaway: override = runtime choice; new = compile-time hiding (avoid). Prefer interfaces + composition; seal what is not designed for extension.

questionText: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class, and how do you choose?
shortAnswer: Interface = pure capability contract, multiple allowed, no state (until default members); abstract class = shared lineage with state and shared implementation, single inheritance. Default to interfaces; reach for abstract classes for versioned frameworks with common code.
detailedAnswer: Interfaces (IDisposable, IComparer<T>) declare what implementers can do — a class can implement many, structs can implement them (boxing only when cast to the interface), and they are the unit of mocking and DI registration. Since C# 8, interfaces can carry default implementations + static members (evolution without breaking implementers) and since C# 11 static abstract members (generic math). Abstract classes (Stream, DbContext) capture an is-a family: shared fields, constructors, non-virtual helpers, and protected members for subclasses — but single inheritance only, and they impose a base type on every consumer. Decision guide: defining a capability used across unrelated types → interface; evolving a framework with shared plumbing + a few customization hooks → abstract class; need state + constructor enforcement → abstract class; test seams and DI boundaries → interfaces; multiple behaviors on one type → interfaces (a type can be both disposable and comparable). Modern .NET leans interface-first (minimal APIs, options, middleware all compose via interfaces/delegates), with abstract classes reserved for genuine hierarchies.
internalWorking: Interface dispatch uses interface maps (slightly costlier than virtual slots historically; JIT-optimized for monomorphic call sites). Abstract-class calls are ordinary virtual dispatch. Default interface methods complicate the map (reabstraction rules) but remain JIT-friendly.
realWorldUsage: DI registrations (services.AddScoped<INotifier, EmailNotifier>), repository abstractions, strategy families, and test doubles — interfaces at every seam.
commonMistake: Abstract class with only abstract members (should be an interface), fat interfaces violated by half the implementers (split them — Interface Segregation), and default interface methods used as a backdoor for shared state (not supported — state still needs the class).
technicalConversation: Ask what breaks when a v2 member is added to a widely-implemented interface — then introduce default implementations as the answer, with the caveat that diamond ambiguities must be resolved explicitly.
interviewFollowUp: How do static abstract interface members enable generic math, and why couldn't abstract classes do it?
keyTakeaway: Interfaces define capabilities across unrelated types; abstract classes share lineage and code. Interface-first, abstract for true families.

questionText: What does 'favor composition over inheritance' mean, and what does it look like in practice?
shortAnswer: Build behavior by combining small parts (has-a) instead of inheriting it (is-a). Composition isolates change: swap a strategy, decorate a capability, or reuse a component without disturbing a fragile base-class hierarchy.
detailedAnswer: Inheritance couples you to the base class's entire surface and its future changes (fragile base class problem: a base-class 'optimization' silently breaks subclasses; the wrong override runs because of new-vs-override). Composition inverts this: a class owns collaborators via interfaces and delegates work. The three patterns: Strategy (OrderPricer takes IDiscountPolicy — new discounts = new classes, zero edits), Decorator (CachingNotifier wraps INotifier — behavior stacks without subclasses), and plain delegation (Controller takes services, not a GodBaseController). Inheritance remains right for true is-a with substitutability (exceptions, Stream subtypes honoring the contract — Liskov). Refactoring cue: hierarchies deeper than two, subclasses overriding to disable base behavior (Square-vs-Rectangle area problem), or switch-on-type beside a hierarchy (polymorphism wanted). DI containers make composition ergonomic: constructors declare needs, lifetimes manage sharing — the modern codebase is a composition graph, with inheritance used sparingly for frameworks' extension points.
internalWorking: No runtime difference of consequence — both compile to interface/virtual calls. The benefit is entirely architectural: smaller blast radius per change, independent testing of parts (mock IDiscountPolicy alone), and no vtable-coupling to base internals.
realWorldUsage: ASP.NET Core itself (middleware pipeline composes delegates; filters compose attributes), pricing/tax/shipping rule engines, notification channels, and validation rule sets.
commonMistake: Service-locator or static access disguised as composition (hidden coupling), constructor over-injection (6+ dependencies signals the class does too much — facade or split), and decorating without preserving the interface (leaky wrappers).
technicalConversation: Ask them to redesign a 4-level controller hierarchy with composition — shared behavior becomes services/filters, leaving thin controllers. The hesitation points reveal hierarchy comfort zones.
interviewFollowUp: When is inheritance genuinely the better tool — give a concrete example and defend it against a composition rewrite.
keyTakeaway: Compose behaviors, inherit only true substitutable lineage. DI + strategy/decorator cover nearly every 'reuse' need without the fragility.

questionText: Explain SOLID with one concrete C# example for each principle.
shortAnswer: S: one reason to change per class. O: extend via new code, not edits (strategy/plugin). L: subclasses must honor base contracts. I: small focused interfaces over fat ones. D: depend on abstractions (constructor-injected interfaces), not concretions.
detailedAnswer: Single Responsibility: an OrderService that prices, persists, emails, and logs has four reasons to change — split into Pricer, Repository, Notifier (each changes for one stakeholder reason). Open/Closed: new discount types arrive as new IDiscountPolicy implementations, not edits to a switch — the pricer is closed for modification, open for extension (decorators extend without touching). Liskov Substitution: a ReadOnlyRepository throwing on Save breaks Repository consumers — substitutability means preconditions cannot strengthen, postconditions cannot weaken (the Square/Rectangle trap: Square.SetWidth breaking area math). Interface Segregation: IWorker with Work/Eat split into IWorkable/IFeedable so robots don't implement Eat — clients depend only on what they use. Dependency Inversion: OrderController takes INotifier (abstraction, injected) not SmtpNotifier (concretion, newed) — high-level policy independent of low-level detail, testable via mocks. SOLID is a means to low coupling and safe change, not a checklist: a 20-line script needs none of it; a payment module needs all of it. Over-application (ISingleMethodEverything interfaces, speculative seams) is the common failure mode — apply at module boundaries under real change pressure.
internalWorking: No runtime footprint — SOLID is design-time structure. Its runtime enablers are interfaces, virtual dispatch, and DI containers (composition roots wiring abstractions to implementations).
realWorldUsage: Payment/shipping provider plug-ins (O), testable services via constructor injection (D), role-based capability interfaces (I), substitutable repository decorators (L), and single-purpose domain services (S).
commonMistake: Cargo-cult SOLID: interfaces for every class (noise), Liskov violations via NotSupportedException in overrides, and SRP interpreted as 'one method per class' instead of 'one reason to change'.
technicalConversation: Ask which principle a God-class violates and what the first split would be — then which principle the split itself demonstrates (usually S first, D second).
interviewFollowUp: Give an example where strictly following OCP (never editing) would be worse than a simple edit.
keyTakeaway: SOLID = change-safe design: single reasons, extension without edits, substitutable parts, lean contracts, abstracted dependencies. Apply under real change pressure.

questionText: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle, and what does a violation look like in production?
shortAnswer: Subtypes must be usable wherever their base type is expected, without breaking caller assumptions. Violations: overrides that throw NotSupportedException, strengthen preconditions, or weaken postconditions — production symptom is code that works for the base but fails for a specific subclass.
detailedAnswer: Formally: preconditions cannot be strengthened (a subclass cannot demand more), postconditions cannot be weakened (cannot promise less), invariants must hold, and history constraints respected. Classic violations: Square : Rectangle overriding area math so SetWidth breaks height assumptions; ReadOnlyFileStream : Stream throwing on Write (Stream promises writable-or-check-CanWrite — the CanWrite guard is the contract's escape hatch, and callers that skip it break); a DiscountPolicy returning negative totals when the contract says 0..subtotal. Production shape: a new provider/tenant-specific subclass passes unit tests (tested in isolation) but breaks the shared pipeline (assumptions encoded in the pipeline, not the tests) — e.g. a BulkOrder subclass that throws on expedited shipping inside a checkout flow that assumes all orders can expedite. Defenses: contract tests (same suite runs against every implementation), CanXxx capability properties (Stream.CanWrite) honored by callers, composition instead of subtyping when behaviors genuinely differ, and code review that asks 'what does the base promise?' for every override. LSP is also the reason preferring interfaces helps: narrower contracts are easier to honor fully.
internalWorking: No IL-level concept — LSP is verified by reasoning and tests, not the compiler (except via nullable annotations and variance rules, which enforce narrow slices of it). Design-by-contract tools can assert pre/postconditions at runtime during testing.
realWorldUsage: Payment/shipping provider hierarchies, multi-tenant feature variations, test doubles (a mock that accepts anything the real rejects hides bugs — strict mocks exist for this), and EF provider differences (SQLite vs SQL Server honoring the same LINQ surface, mostly).
commonMistake: NotSupportedException in overrides (the canonical smell), subclass-only members downcast by callers (if (x is BulkOrder b) — the hierarchy failed), and 'harmless' precondition tightening (non-null where base allowed null) breaking existing callers.
technicalConversation: Ask how they would catch an LSP violation before production — contract test suites executed per implementation is the senior answer; 'careful review' is the junior one.
interviewFollowUp: How do C# nullable reference types enforce a small part of LSP at compile time?
keyTakeaway: Subtypes must honor base promises exactly. Throwing overrides and tightened preconditions are the smell; contract tests are the defense.

questionText: What is Dependency Inversion, and how does it differ from Dependency Injection?
shortAnswer: Inversion is the principle (depend on abstractions, not concretions); Injection is the technique (supplying dependencies via constructor/method/container). DI is how you implement DIP — plus a container to wire the graph.
detailedAnswer: Dependency Inversion (the D in SOLID): high-level modules (CheckoutService) and low-level modules (SmtpNotifier) should both depend on abstractions (INotifier); abstractions should not depend on details. This flips the naive direction where policy depends on plumbing. Dependency Injection is the delivery mechanism: constructor injection (required collaborators — preferred, makes requirements explicit and the object always valid), method/parameter injection (per-call data like CancellationToken), and property injection (optional, defaultable — use rarely, it hides requirements). The container (Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection) is the third piece: registration (AddScoped<INotifier, SmtpNotifier>), resolution (the composition root builds the graph), and lifetime management (transient/scoped/singleton). Without inversion, injection is just plumbing (passing concretions); without injection, inversion is just interfaces nobody wires. Testing is the immediate payoff (mock INotifier), but the architectural payoff is independent deployability of policy vs adapters (ports-and-adapters/hexagonal is DIP at scale). Lifetime interplay matters: injecting a scoped service into a singleton (captive dependency) is a DIP-wired bug — the principle doesn't save you from the container's rules.
internalWorking: No runtime magic beyond virtual dispatch: the container uses compiled expression trees / dynamic methods to construct graphs fast after the first resolution (registrations validate at startup with ValidateOnBuild in dev). Lifetimes are scope dictionaries — scoped = per-scope instance cache.
realWorldUsage: Every ASP.NET Core app (controllers take services, middleware takes options), test suites (substitute fakes), and modular monoliths (feature modules behind port interfaces).
commonMistake: Confusing the terms (calling constructor parameters 'inversion'), new-ing concretions inside services (inversion violated regardless of interfaces existing elsewhere), service-locator pattern (hides dependencies, untestable), and captive dependencies (scoped-in-singleton).
technicalConversation: Ask them to find the inversion in a codebase: interfaces owned by the consumer (policy side), implementations in adapter projects, container wiring at the edge. If interfaces live next to implementations, inversion is likely absent.
interviewFollowUp: Why should the abstraction (interface) be owned by the high-level policy rather than the low-level adapter?
keyTakeaway: Inversion = depend on abstractions; Injection = supply via constructor; Container = wire + lifetime. Together they decouple policy from plumbing.

questionText: What are access modifiers in C#, and how do you use internal and protected internal correctly?
shortAnswer: public (everyone), private (own type), protected (subclasses), internal (same assembly), private protected (subclass + same assembly), protected internal (subclass OR same assembly). Use internal for helpers that shouldn't leak past the assembly boundary; protected internal is the union — rarely what you want.
detailedAnswer: The six levels form a lattice: private < (private protected, internal) < protected internal < public, with protected on its own axis. Defaults: class members private, top-level types internal. Practical usage: public = supported API surface (needs docs + stability); internal = implementation shared within a project (repositories' helpers, infrastructure details) — combine with InternalsVisibleTo for tests to keep the public surface honest; protected = extension points for subclasses (template-method hooks); private protected = subclass access restricted to your own assembly (framework designs); protected internal = union of protected and internal — commonly misunderstood as intersection (it is OR, not AND). Assembly boundaries are the key mental model: internal draws the encapsulation line at the project, which is why Domain keeps public entities but Infrastructure exposes only what Api needs. Records/classes default internal for a reason — start closed, open deliberately. Reflection and InternalsVisibleTo can cross lines (tests, serializers); treat those as explicit exceptions, not habits.
internalWorking: Accessibility is metadata (Family/Assembly flags) enforced by the JIT/verifier at call time — no runtime cost. internal is assembly-identity based (same compiled assembly, or friend assemblies via InternalsVisibleTo with strong-name matching when signed).
realWorldUsage: Keeping Infrastructure types internal while exposing extension methods (AddInfrastructure), test-only hooks via InternalsVisibleTo, and SDK design (public surface vs internal plumbing).
commonMistake: Everything public 'for convenience' (surface you must support forever), protected fields (couple subclasses to representation), and protected internal assumed to mean 'subclasses in my assembly' (it means the union — use private protected for that).
technicalConversation: Ask what their test project accesses — if tests need lots of publics, the seam is wrong; InternalsVisibleTo or testing through public behavior are the two honest answers.
interviewFollowUp: Why do top-level types default to internal rather than public?
keyTakeaway: Start closed (private/internal), open deliberately. internal = assembly encapsulation; protected internal is a union, not an intersection.

questionText: What is the decorator pattern, and how does it compare to inheritance for adding behavior?
shortAnswer: Decorator wraps an interface implementation to add behavior (logging, caching, validation) while remaining substitutable. Unlike inheritance, decorators stack in any combination at runtime, need no subclass per combination, and never touch the wrapped class.
detailedAnswer: Structure: LoggingNotifier(INotifier inner) implements INotifier, logs, then calls inner.SendAsync — registration decides the stack (AddScoped<INotifier, SmtpNotifier> then decorate). Combinations multiply freely: caching + retry + logging + metrics = 4 small classes composed in any order, versus 2^4 subclasses. Order matters (cache outside retry? retry outside logging?) and should be explicit in composition-root registration. Compared to inheritance: no fragile base, no vtable coupling, behaviors testable in isolation (wrap a fake inner). Compared to middleware/filters: same idea at different layers (ASP.NET middleware decorates requests; decorators decorate services). Costs: one interface + one class per behavior (boilerplate, mitigated by source-generated or Scrutor's Decorate()), and deep stacks complicate debugging (name wrappers clearly, log the chain at startup in dev). Scrutor (services.Decorate<INotifier, CachingNotifier>()) makes registration one line. Repository + caching + logging is the canonical business-app stack.
internalWorking: Plain interface dispatch per layer — negligible overhead (one virtual call each). Scrutor generates the closed-generic wiring at startup via expression compilation; no runtime proxies unless you add Castle (virtual-method interception, heavier — prefer explicit decorators).
realWorldUsage: Cross-cutting service behavior (caching repositories, retrying gateways, auditing commands), MediatR pipeline behaviors (validation/logging around handlers), and ASP.NET response caching at the service layer.
commonMistake: Decorating IDisposable chains incorrectly (who disposes inner? — container owns the graph, don't dispose manually), order-dependent bugs (logging inside retry hides attempts), and decorating with concrete types (always decorate the interface).
technicalConversation: Ask them to add metrics to an existing cached repository without touching either class — the one-class decorator is the answer, and registration order is the follow-up.
interviewFollowUp: How do MediatR pipeline behaviors relate to the decorator pattern?
keyTakeaway: Decorate interfaces to stack behavior without subclasses. Explicit registration order, isolated tests, container-owned lifetimes.

questionText: What is method overloading vs overriding, and what are the resolution rules?
shortAnswer: Overloading = same name, different signatures, resolved at compile time (can coexist in one class). Overriding = replacing a virtual/abstract base implementation, resolved at runtime by actual type. Overloads differ by parameter types/count (not return type alone).
detailedAnswer: Overloading is compile-time selection: the compiler picks the best match by argument types, with implicit conversions, optional parameters, params arrays, and named arguments complicating the ranking (better-function-member rules; ambiguous calls are compile errors, occasionally surprising with null literals or numeric overloads — prefer explicit casts at call sites). Overloads can differ in static/instance? No — same name different arity/types; return type alone never distinguishes (why: callers may ignore returns). Overriding is runtime dispatch through virtual slots (see virtual/override). The two interact: a derived class adding an overload hides base overloads by name (method hiding by signature — base.Print(int) invisible when derived declares Print(string) unless base. qualified; another hiding footgun). API design guidance: overloads should do the same thing with different inputs (Parse(string) vs Parse(ReadOnlySpan<char>)); different behaviors deserve different names. Optional parameters vs overloads: optionals keep one method (versioning risk — defaults bake into callers at compile time, so changing a default requires recompiling consumers; libraries prefer overloads). params + overloads + generics together can create ambiguity — test the call shapes you promise.
internalWorking: Overloads are separate methods (separate slots/metadata); selection is entirely frontend overload resolution emitting a direct call. Overrides share the virtual slot; the object's method table picks the implementation per call (one indirection, devirtualizable when sealed).
realWorldUsage: Logger APIs, constructor overloads (DI-friendly greediest + simple), mininal-API handler shapes, and serialization entry points (Serialize<T>(T) vs Serialize(object, Type)).
commonMistake: Overload that differs only by optional parameter (ambiguous with another overload), changing an optional default in a library (callers keep the old baked-in value), and 'overloads' that do unrelated things (name them differently).
technicalConversation: Ask why C# forbids overloads differing only by return type — overload resolution happens before the return value is considered (and callers can discard it).
interviewFollowUp: How do named arguments and params arrays complicate overload resolution, and how do you keep APIs unambiguous?
keyTakeaway: Overload = compile-time choice by signature; override = runtime choice by type. Same behavior per name; defaults bake into callers.
